lessons.title: Key Moments — White Shoppers & Bus Explosion

before.content_html:
Key Moment One: White Shoppers Scene

The White Shoppers scene takes place at Forsythe & Sons grocery store (timestamp 13:50 in the recorded version). It begins with the line “Next stop, Anniston, Alabama.” This scene introduces the Little White Girl (LWG) and reveals the casual, everyday racism that the Freedom Riders were fighting against.

Positioning and Staging

The LWG (a 12-year-old character) sat on a tall stool centre stage. The White shoppers were positioned upstage right (USR) while they put on their white gloves, then took a step in — reducing proxemics — on the name of the store to highlight the location to the audience. The LWG’s mum was positioned upstage left (USL).

Three steel flats at the back of the space represented the Greyhound bus the Freedom Riders were travelling on. Only the tall stool centre stage was used in this scene, with small stools positioned stage left and stage right, and a tall stool at the back of the space USR.

Key Fact — Why Positioning Matters

The LWG being placed on the tall stool centre stage made her the focal point of the scene. This positioning highlighted her innocence and the significance of her questioning of racism. The White shoppers staying USL showed they were a united group, separate from the LWG, reinforcing that racist attitudes were normalised in this community.

Voice Techniques in the White Shoppers Scene

The White female shoppers spoke in a high pitch and in unison: “we do, we do.” This suggested their opinions were identical. The high pitch suggested to the audience that they were “air heads” who did not think for themselves.

The LWG’s mum said “the coloured folk can do their shopping down their part of town” — here “their” was emphasised by elongating the word. This drew the audience’s attention to the discrimination the Freedom Riders were fighting against.

When the LWG questioned “why?” she used a higher pitch at the end of the word to show she was genuinely questioning her mum. This demonstrated to the audience that the child could not see any reason why people should be treated differently because of their colour.

The mum replied “just different honey, that’s all you need to know” using a high pitch, which suggested she had no real justification for her answer and highlighted her lack of education on the subject. The shoppers then spoke “We’re happy” in unison, again using a very high-pitched voice to reinforce they were not thinking independently.

Physicality in the White Shoppers Scene

The White female shoppers stood in very close proximity of one another, linking their arms as if they were one person. They aggressively fanned the hand covered in the white glove — a quick-paced movement that was echoed by the LWG’s mum. The LWG’s mum emphasised “their” further with a double flick of the wrist in a derogatory fashion, as if dismissing someone, suggesting she felt that Black people were beneath her.

When the LWG said “why?”, all attention was placed on her. Em and Dayz immediately stopped fanning and made direct eye contact with the LWG. The mum moved her head sharply to stare at the LWG — this physicality showed the performers were shocked at the question, because it was not in line with their racist thinking.

Key Fact — Costume Detail

The only addition to the base costumes in this scene was a single white glove for each female performer playing a White shopper. Dayz put on the left-hand glove and Em put on the right-hand glove — reinforcing that they “are as one” and that their racist thinking was aligned. Ty had no costume change but used physicality changes (holding hands pinched together at waist height) to create his character.

A white and blue lighting wash was used at the start of the scene. The blue tinge was emphasised by the reflection of the steel flats, suggesting loneliness and isolation for the Freedom Riders. When the line “Such a beautiful day” was spoken, the white light intensity increased and the blue was removed, symbolising the sun through the bus window.

When the LWG was introduced, the white lighting wash increased in intensity and the blue colour was removed entirely. This bright white lighting symbolised the innocence of the LWG and her purity.

Key Moment Two: The Bus Explosion Scene

The bus explosion scene (timestamp 15:54) begins with Uncle George shouting “Hey, Hey!” This scene depicts the violent attack on the Freedom Riders’ bus when it reached Anniston, Alabama. It is one of the most powerful moments in the performance, building to an intense climax.

Positioning and Levels in the Bus Explosion

Centre stage left, a small stool and a tall stool were placed directly next to one another in close proxemics. Uncle George (played by Ty) stood with one leg on the tall stool and one on the small stool, widening his gait to make the character seem larger, more imposing, and more intimidating. His position on the highest level signified his power as the ringleader of the White mob.

USR, CJ sat on the tall stool looking directly at Uncle George. Em stood in front of a small stool almost centre of stage right, watching the actor in role as Uncle George. Dayz stood downstage left with her back to the audience. All actors having direct eye contact on Uncle George showed he was the most significant character in this moment.

On the line “Hey, stop, stop ’em, that bus with Yankees, Jews and uppity blacks sitting in the wrong place,” Uncle George outstretched his right arm using strong muscle tension and a pointing gesture, directing the audience’s attention to the bus and showing his anger was aimed at everyone on board. He used an aggressive tone, quick pace, and loud volume.

On “We’ll show them their place,” UG stepped onto the highest stool and tensed both fists at his sides in an intimidating fashion. Contrastingly, this line was spoken in a quieter volume with a calm tone, as if UG had the right to decide who could visit his hometown — highlighting his ignorance and lack of empathy.

On “No darks and Yankee’s are going to tell us how to behave,” he used a quick-paced pointing gesture at himself with his thumb while his hand remained in a fist — the fist “threatened” the Freedom Riders. The emphasis on “us” was created by a short pause before and after the word.

The Freedom Riders on the Bus

When Dayz and Em took on the roles of Freedom Riders, they each took a small stool and placed them in close proximity centre stage, gripping the sides with very strong muscle tension as if holding on to the edge of their seats on the bus. This simple physicality helped the audience imagine the bus clearly, creating empathy.

Dayz used quick-paced breaths and exaggerated shoulder movements to show fear, with fidgety movements as she looked around for comfort. In contrast, Em’s Freedom Rider was much more static and composed, sitting facing forward and making direct eye contact with the audience whilst reciting the Lord’s Prayer. This contrast in physicality effectively highlighted the panic of the situation and how different people react differently when faced with the same danger.

Key Fact — Ensemble Movement and Slow Motion

During the explosion, Em and Dayz moved their arms up to protect their heads in slow motion. This was effective because it marked the most serious moment and symbolised that the Freedom Riders were not violent — their movement was a passive protest. Using slow motion rather than having the characters fall to the floor suggested they had not lost any power by remaining non-violent.

Lighting: When UG said “Throw it in” and “burn ’em, burn ’em alive,” a small orange shaft of light appeared USC on the middle steel flat, showing the audience the bus was now alight. The intensity increased gradually until “the engine’s going to blow” when the orange reached its peak. The white wash faded to a much lower intensity, making the orange flames stand out. The orange light created shadows on the flats, creating the illusion of a crowd of Freedom Riders — making the audience feel there were many people in danger.

Sound: A banging sound effect was used as if someone was banging on the side of the bus, emphasised by the Freedom Riders asking “What’s that noise?” Faint sounds of a crowd talking and small bangs built gradually. A small explosion sound was used when UG said “the engine’s going to blow.” A sound collage built the climax: Em repeated the Lord’s Prayer, UG shouted “burn, negro lovers, burn,” the LWG narrated, and Dayz panicked saying “they’re going to burn us alive.”
